title: Book 7, Chapter 21 — Eighteenth and Nineteenth Years of the War—Arrival of Gylippus at Syracuse—Fortification of Decelea—Successes of the Syracusans
paragraphs: Gylippus and Pythen refitted their ships and coasted from Tarentum to Epizephyrian Locris. There they received more accurate information: Syracuse was not yet completely walled in, and an army that reached Epipolae could still force its way into the city. They therefore debated two courses. They could keep Sicily on their right and risk sailing in by sea. Or they could keep it on their left, sail first to Himera, take with them the Himeraeans and any others who agreed to join, and go to Syracuse by land. They decided to sail for Himera, particularly because the four Athenian ships that Nicias had at last sent off, on hearing that they were at Locris, had not yet arrived at Rhegium. So before those ships reached their station, the Peloponnesians crossed the strait, touched at Rhegium and Messina, and came to Himera. There they persuaded the Himeraeans to join the war, to go with them in person, and to supply arms to the seamen from their ships, which they had hauled ashore at Himera. They also sent word to the Selinuntines to meet them at an appointed place with all their forces. The Geloans and some of the Sicels promised a few troops. These Sicels were now much readier to join them, because Archonidas, a powerful Sicel king in that region and a friend of Athens, had recently died, and because Gylippus had shown such energy in coming from Lacedaemon. Gylippus took with him about seven hundred of his sailors and marines (that was all the number for which he had arms), a thousand heavy infantry and light troops from Himera with a hundred horse, some light troops and cavalry from Selinus, a few Geloans, and Sicels numbering a thousand in all. With these he set out on his march for Syracuse.

Meanwhile the Corinthian fleet from Leucas hurried to arrive. One of its commanders, Gongylus, started last with a single ship, yet reached Syracuse first, a little before Gylippus. He found the Syracusans about to hold an assembly to consider whether to end the war. He prevented this and reassured them, telling them that more ships were still to come and that the Lacedaemonians had sent Gylippus, son of Cleandridas, to take command. At this the Syracusans took courage and at once marched out with all their forces to meet Gylippus, whom they found to be close at hand. Gylippus, after taking on his way Ietae, a fort of the Sicels, drew up his army in order of battle. He reached Epipolae, ascended by Euryelus, as the Athenians had done at first, and advanced with the Syracusans against the Athenian lines. He arrived at a critical moment. The Athenians had already completed a double wall of six or seven furlongs toward the great harbor, except for a small stretch next to the sea, on which they were still working. In the rest of the circle, toward Trogilus on the other sea, stones had been laid ready for building along most of the distance; some points had been left half finished, and others were entirely complete. The danger to Syracuse had indeed been great.

The Athenians recovered from the confusion into which the sudden approach of Gylippus and the Syracusans had first thrown them, and formed in order of battle. Gylippus halted a short distance away and sent a herald to tell them that, if they would evacuate Sicily with all their belongings within five days, he was willing to make a truce on those terms. The Athenians treated the proposal with contempt and dismissed the herald without an answer. Both sides then began to prepare for action. Gylippus saw that the Syracusans were in disorder and did not easily fall into line, so he drew his troops back onto more open ground. Nicias did not lead the Athenians forward but stayed still by his own wall. When Gylippus saw that they would not come on, he led his army off to the citadel of the quarter of Apollo Temenites and spent the night there. On the following day he led out the main body of his army and drew it up in order of battle before the Athenian walls, to prevent the Athenians from going to the relief of any other quarter. He dispatched a strong force against Fort Labdalum and took it, putting to the sword everyone he found inside; the place was not within sight of the Athenians. On the same day the Syracusans also captured an Athenian galley that lay moored off the harbor.

After this the Syracusans and their allies began to carry a single wall from the city up Epipolae in a slanting direction, so that the Athenians, unless they could hinder the work, would no longer be able to invest them. The Athenians, meanwhile, had finished their wall down to the sea and had come up to the heights. Part of their wall was weak, and Gylippus led out his army by night and attacked it. But the Athenians who happened to be bivouacking outside took the alarm and came out to meet him, and when he saw this he quickly led his men back. The Athenians then built their wall higher, and from then on kept guard at this point themselves, posting their confederates along the rest of the works at the stations assigned to them. Nicias also decided to fortify Plemmyrium, a promontory opposite the city, which juts out and narrows the mouth of the Great Harbor. He thought that fortifying it would make it easier to bring in supplies. They would be able to maintain their blockade from a shorter distance, near the port held by the Syracusans, instead of having to put out from the bottom of the great harbor against the enemy’s navy at every movement it made. He was also paying more attention now to the war by sea, since the coming of Gylippus had diminished their hopes by land. So he conveyed over his ships and some troops, and built three forts, in which he placed most of his baggage; from then on he kept the larger craft and warships moored there. This was the first and chief cause of the losses suffered by the crews. The water they used was scarce and had to be fetched from far away, and the sailors could not go out for firewood without being cut off by the Syracusan horse, who were masters of the country. A third of the enemy’s cavalry was stationed at the little town of Olympieum to prevent plundering raids by the Athenians at Plemmyrium. Meanwhile Nicias learned that the rest of the Corinthian fleet was approaching, and he sent twenty ships to watch for it, with orders to keep a lookout about Locris and Rhegium and the approach to Sicily.

Gylippus, for his part, went on with the wall across Epipolae, using the stones the Athenians had laid down for their own wall. At the same time he constantly led out the Syracusans and their allies and formed them in order of battle in front of the lines, while the Athenians formed up against him. At last he judged that the moment had come and began the attack. A hand-to-hand fight followed between the lines, where the Syracusan cavalry could be of no use. The Syracusans and their allies were defeated and took up their dead under truce, and the Athenians erected a trophy. After this Gylippus called the soldiers together and told them that the fault was not theirs but his. He had kept their lines too much within the works and had thus deprived them of the services of their cavalry and darters. He would now lead them on a second time. He begged them to remember that in material force they would be fully a match for their opponents. As for moral advantages, it would be intolerable if Peloponnesians and Dorians did not feel confident of overcoming Ionians and islanders, with the motley rabble that accompanied them, and of driving them out of the country.

After this he took the first opportunity that offered to lead them against the enemy again. Nicias and the Athenians held that, even if the Syracusans did not wish to offer battle, they had to prevent the building of the cross wall. It already almost overlapped the extreme point of their own wall, and if it went any further it would make no difference from then on whether they won ever so many battles or never fought at all. So they came out to meet the Syracusans. Gylippus led his heavy infantry out farther from the fortifications than on the former occasion and so joined battle. He posted his horse and darters on the flank of the Athenians, in the open space where the works of the two walls ended. During the engagement the cavalry attacked and routed the left wing of the Athenians, which was opposed to it, and as a result the rest of the Athenian army was beaten by the Syracusans and driven headlong within its lines. The following night the Syracusans carried their wall up to the Athenian works and past them. This put it out of the Athenians’ power to stop them any longer, and deprived them, even if victorious in the field, of all chance of investing the city in the future.

After this the remaining twelve ships of the Corinthians, Ambraciots and Leucadians, under the command of Erasinides, a Corinthian, sailed into the harbor, having eluded the Athenian ships on guard, and helped the Syracusans to complete the rest of the cross wall. Gylippus meanwhile went into the rest of Sicily to raise land and naval forces, and also to bring over any cities that were either lukewarm in the cause or had so far kept out of the war altogether. Syracusan and Corinthian envoys were also dispatched to Lacedaemon and Corinth to have a fresh force sent over by any means that offered, whether in merchant vessels or transports or in any other way likely to succeed, since the Athenians too were sending for reinforcements. The Syracusans, for their part, proceeded to man a fleet and to exercise it, meaning to try their fortune in this way also, and in general they became exceedingly confident.

Nicias saw this. He also saw the strength of the enemy and his own difficulties growing daily, and he too sent to Athens. He had often sent reports before, as events occurred, but he felt it especially incumbent on him to do so now, since he thought that they were in a critical position and that, unless they were speedily recalled or strongly reinforced from home, they had no hope of safety. He feared, however, that the messengers might not report the truth, whether through inability to speak, or failure of memory, or a wish to please the multitude. So he thought it best to write a letter, to make sure that the Athenians would know his own opinion without its being lost in transmission, and would be able to decide on the real facts of the case.

His emissaries accordingly departed with the letter and the necessary verbal instructions. He himself attended to the affairs of the army, making it his aim now to keep on the defensive and to avoid any unnecessary danger.

At the close of the same summer the Athenian general Euetion marched with a large body of Thracians, together with Perdiccas, against Amphipolis. He failed to take it, but he brought some galleys round into the Strymon and blockaded the town from the river, with his base at Himeraeum.

Summer was now over. In the winter that followed, the men sent by Nicias reached Athens, gave the verbal messages entrusted to them, answered the questions that were put to them, and delivered the letter. The clerk of the city then came forward and read it out to the Athenians. It was as follows:

“Athenians, many other letters have made our past operations known to you. It is now time for you to become equally familiar with our present condition and to take your measures accordingly. In most of our engagements with the Syracusans, against whom we were sent, we had defeated them, and we had built the works that we now occupy. Then Gylippus arrived from Lacedaemon with an army drawn from Peloponnese and from some of the cities in Sicily. In our first battle with him we were victorious. In the battle on the following day we were overpowered by a multitude of cavalry and darters and compelled to retire within our lines. The numbers opposed to us have therefore forced us to give up the work of circumvallation and to remain inactive. We cannot even make use of all the force we have, since a large part of our heavy infantry is absorbed in the defense of our lines. Meanwhile the enemy have carried a single wall past our lines. This makes it impossible for us to invest them in future, unless a strong force attacks and captures this cross wall. So the besieger in name has become, at least from the land side, the besieged in reality, since their cavalry prevents us from going for any distance into the country.

“Besides this, an embassy has been dispatched to Peloponnese to procure reinforcements, and Gylippus has gone to the cities in Sicily. He hopes partly to induce those that are at present neutral to join him in the war, and partly to bring from his allies additional contingents for the land forces and material for the navy. For I understand that they contemplate a combined attack on our lines, with their land forces and with their fleet by sea. None of you must be surprised that I say by sea also. They have discovered that the length of time we have now been in commission has rotted our ships and wasted our crews, and that with the soundness of our ships and the full strength of our crews the pristine efficiency of our navy has departed. For it is impossible for us to haul our ships ashore and careen them. The enemy’s vessels are as many as ours or more, and we are constantly expecting an attack. Indeed, they can be seen exercising, and it lies with them to take the initiative; and since they do not have to maintain a blockade, they have greater facilities for drying their ships.

“We could scarcely do this even if we had plenty of ships to spare and were free of our present necessity of exhausting all our strength on the blockade. For it is already difficult to carry in supplies past Syracuse, and if we relaxed our vigilance in the slightest degree it would become impossible. The losses that our crews have suffered, and still suffer, come from the following causes. Expeditions for fuel and for forage, and the distance from which water has to be fetched, cause our sailors to be cut off by the Syracusan cavalry. The loss of our previous superiority emboldens our slaves to desert. Our foreign seamen are impressed by the unexpected appearance of a navy against us and by the strength of the enemy’s resistance. Those of them who were pressed into the service take the first opportunity of departing to their respective cities. Those who were originally seduced by the temptation of high pay, and expected little fighting and large gains, leave us either by deserting to the enemy or by using one or other of the various means of escape that the size of Sicily affords them. Some even engage in trade themselves and persuade the captains to take Hyccaric slaves on board in their place. In this way they have ruined the efficiency of our navy.

“I need not remind you that the time during which a crew is in its prime is short, and that few sailors can start a ship on her way and keep the rowing in time. But by far my greatest trouble is this. Holding the post I do, I am prevented by the natural indocility of the Athenian seaman from putting a stop to these evils. Meanwhile we have no source from which to recruit our crews, which the enemy can do from many quarters. We are compelled to depend, both for supplying the crews in service and for making good our losses, on the men we brought with us. For our present confederates, Naxos and Catana, are incapable of supplying us. Only one thing more is wanting to our opponents, I mean the defection of our Italian markets. If they were to see you neglect to relieve us from our present condition, and were to go over to the enemy, famine would compel us to evacuate, and Syracuse would finish the war without a blow.

“I might, it is true, have written to you something different and more agreeable than this, but certainly nothing more useful, if you need to know the real state of things here before taking your measures. Besides, I know that it is your nature to love to be told the best side of things, and then to blame the teller if the result does not answer the expectations he has raised in your minds. I therefore thought it safest to declare the truth to you.

“Now you are not to think that either your generals or your soldiers have ceased to be a match for the forces originally opposed to them. But you are to reflect that a general Sicilian coalition is being formed against us, that a fresh army is expected from Peloponnese, and that the force we have here cannot cope even with our present antagonists. You must promptly decide either to recall us or to send out to us another fleet and army as numerous again, with a large sum of money, and someone to succeed me, since a disease in the kidneys makes me unfit to keep my post. I think I have some claim on your indulgence, for while I was in my prime I did you much good service in my commands. But whatever you mean to do, do it at the beginning of spring and without delay. The enemy will obtain his Sicilian reinforcements shortly, and those from Peloponnese after a longer interval. Unless you attend to the matter, the former will be here before you, while the latter will elude you as they have done before.”

Such were the contents of Nicias’s letter. When the Athenians had heard it, they refused to accept his resignation. Instead they chose him two colleagues, naming Menander and Euthydemus, two of the officers at the seat of war, to fill their places until the others arrived, so that Nicias would not be left alone in his sickness to bear the whole weight of affairs. They also voted to send out another army and navy, drawn partly from the Athenians on the muster-roll and partly from the allies. The colleagues chosen for Nicias were Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. Eurymedon was sent off at once, about the time of the winter solstice, with ten ships and a hundred and twenty talents of silver, and with instructions to tell the army that reinforcements would arrive and that care would be taken of them. Demosthenes stayed behind to organize the expedition. He meant to start as soon as it was spring, sent to the allies for troops, and meanwhile got together money, ships and heavy infantry at home.

The Athenians also sent twenty ships round Peloponnese to prevent anyone from crossing over to Sicily from Corinth or Peloponnese. The Corinthians had been filled with confidence by the favorable change in Sicilian affairs that the envoys reported on their arrival, and were convinced that the fleet they had sent out before had not been without its use. They were now preparing to dispatch a force of heavy infantry to Sicily in merchant vessels, and the Lacedaemonians were doing the same for the rest of Peloponnese. The Corinthians also manned a fleet of twenty-five ships. They intended to try the result of a battle with the squadron on guard at Naupactus, and meanwhile to make it harder for the Athenians there to hinder the departure of their merchantmen, by forcing them to keep an eye on the galleys arrayed against them.

In the meantime the Lacedaemonians prepared to invade Attica, in accordance with their own earlier resolve and at the instigation of the Syracusans and Corinthians. These wanted an invasion to stop the reinforcements that they heard Athens was about to send to Sicily. Alcibiades also urged them to fortify Decelea and to prosecute the war vigorously. But the Lacedaemonians drew most of their encouragement from two beliefs. One was that Athens, with two wars on her hands, one against themselves and one against the Siceliots, would be easier to subdue. The other was that she had been the first to break the truce. In the former war, they considered, the offense had been more on their own side, both because the Thebans had entered Plataea in time of peace, and because they themselves had refused to listen to the Athenian offer of arbitration, in spite of the clause in the former treaty that where arbitration was offered there should be no appeal to arms. For this reason they thought that they deserved their misfortunes, and they took seriously to heart the disaster at Pylos and whatever else had befallen them. But the ravages from Pylos went on without any intermission. Then the thirty Athenian ships came out from Argos and laid waste part of Epidaurus, Prasiae and other places. And whenever a dispute arose over the interpretation of any doubtful point in the treaty, the Athenians always rejected their offers of arbitration. At length the Lacedaemonians decided that Athens had now committed the very same offense as they had before, and had become the guilty party, and they began to be full of ardor for the war. They spent this winter sending round to their allies for iron and getting ready the other implements for building their fort. Meanwhile they began raising at home, and also by forced requisitions in the rest of Peloponnese, a force to be sent out in the merchantmen to their allies in Sicily. So the winter ended, and with it the eighteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

In the first days of the following spring, earlier than usual, the Lacedaemonians and their allies invaded Attica under the command of Agis, son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians. They began by devastating the parts bordering on the plain, and next proceeded to fortify Decelea, dividing the work among the different cities. Decelea is about thirteen or fourteen miles from the city of Athens, and the same distance or not much farther from Boeotia. The fort was meant to harass the plain and the richest parts of the country, and it was in sight of Athens. While the Peloponnesians and their allies in Attica were busy with the fortification, their countrymen at home sent off, at about the same time, the heavy infantry in the merchant vessels to Sicily. The Lacedaemonians furnished a picked force of Helots and Neodamodes (or freedmen), six hundred heavy infantry in all, under the command of Eccritus, a Spartan. The Boeotians sent three hundred heavy infantry, commanded by two Thebans, Xenon and Nicon, and by Hegesander, a Thespian. These were among the first to put out into the open sea, starting from Taenarus in Laconia. Not long after their departure the Corinthians sent off a force of five hundred heavy infantry, consisting partly of men from Corinth itself and partly of Arcadian mercenaries, under the command of Alexarchus, a Corinthian. The Sicyonians also sent off two hundred heavy infantry at the same time as the Corinthians, under the command of Sargeus, a Sicyonian. Meanwhile the twenty-five ships manned by Corinth during the winter lay facing the twenty Athenian ships at Naupactus, until the heavy infantry in the merchantmen were fairly on their way from Peloponnese. In this way they fulfilled the purpose for which they had been manned originally, which was to divert the attention of the Athenians from the merchantmen to the galleys.

During this time the Athenians were not idle. At the very beginning of spring, at the same time as the fortification of Decelea, they sent thirty ships round Peloponnese under Charicles, son of Apollodorus. He was instructed to call at Argos and demand a force of their heavy infantry for the fleet, as the alliance required. At the same time they dispatched Demosthenes to Sicily, as they had intended, with sixty Athenian and five Chian ships, twelve hundred Athenian heavy infantry from the muster-roll, and as many of the islanders as could be raised in the different quarters. They drew on the other subject allies for whatever they could supply that would be of use for the war. Demosthenes was instructed first to sail round with Charicles and to operate with him on the coasts of Laconia. He accordingly sailed to Aegina and waited there for the rest of his armament, and for Charicles to fetch the Argive troops.

In Sicily, about the same time in this spring, Gylippus came to Syracuse with as many troops as he could bring from the cities he had persuaded to join. He called the Syracusans together and told them that they must man as many ships as possible and try their hand at a sea-fight, by which he hoped to gain an advantage in the war not unworthy of the risk. Hermocrates actively joined him in trying to encourage his countrymen to attack the Athenians at sea. He said that the Athenians had not inherited their naval prowess and would not keep it forever. They had been landsmen even more than the Syracusans, and had become a maritime power only when the Mede forced them. Besides, to daring spirits like the Athenians, a daring adversary would seem the most formidable. The Athenian plan of paralyzing, by the boldness of their attack, a neighbor often not inferior to them in strength could now be used against them with as good effect by the Syracusans. He was convinced also that the unlooked-for sight of Syracusans daring to face the Athenian navy would cause the enemy a terror, whose advantages would far outweigh any loss that Athenian science might inflict on Syracusan inexperience. He therefore urged them to throw aside their fears and to try their fortune at sea. Under the influence of Gylippus and Hermocrates, and perhaps some others, the Syracusans made up their minds for the sea-fight and began to man their ships.

When the fleet was ready, Gylippus led out the whole army by night. His plan was to assault the forts on Plemmyrium in person by land, while thirty-five Syracusan galleys sailed against the enemy from the great harbor as appointed. The remaining forty-five were to come round from the lesser harbor, where they had their arsenal, to join those inside and attack Plemmyrium at the same time, so that the Athenians would be distracted by an assault on two sides at once. The Athenians quickly manned sixty ships. With twenty-five of these they engaged the thirty-five Syracusan ships in the great harbor, and they sent the rest to meet those sailing round from the arsenal. An action ensued directly in front of the mouth of the great harbor, maintained with equal tenacity on both sides, the one wishing to force the passage, the other to prevent it.

In the meantime the Athenians in Plemmyrium had gone down to the sea to attend to the engagement. Gylippus made a sudden attack on the forts in the early morning and took the largest first, and afterwards the two smaller ones, whose garrisons did not wait for him, seeing the largest so easily taken. At the fall of the first fort, the men from it who succeeded in taking refuge in their boats and merchantmen found great difficulty in reaching the camp. The Syracusans were having the best of it in the engagement in the great harbor, and sent a fast-sailing galley to pursue them. But when the two others fell, the Syracusans were being defeated, and the fugitives from these forts sailed along the shore with more ease. The Syracusan ships fighting off the mouth of the harbor forced their way through the Athenian ships and sailed in without any order. They fell foul of one another and handed the victory to the Athenians. The Athenians routed not only this squadron but also the one by which they were at first being defeated in the harbor. They sank eleven of the Syracusan ships and killed most of the men, except the crews of three ships, whom they made prisoners. Their own loss was confined to three ships. They hauled ashore the Syracusan wrecks, set up a trophy on the islet in front of Plemmyrium, and retired to their own camp.

The Syracusans had lost at sea, but they held the forts at Plemmyrium, and for these they set up three trophies. Of the last two forts taken, they tore one down; the other two they repaired and garrisoned. In the capture of the forts a great many men were killed or taken prisoner, and a great quantity of property fell into their hands. The Athenians had used the forts as a storehouse, so there was a large stock of the merchants’ goods and grain inside, and a large stock belonging to the captains as well. The masts and other fittings of forty galleys were taken too, besides three galleys that had been hauled up on shore. Indeed the capture of Plemmyrium was the first and greatest cause of the ruin of the Athenian army. Even the entrance of the harbor was no longer safe for bringing in provisions, because the Syracusan vessels were stationed there to stop them, and nothing could come in without a fight. On top of this came a general dismay and discouragement in the army.

After this the Syracusans sent out twelve ships under Agatharchus, a Syracusan. One of them went to Peloponnese with ambassadors, to describe the hopeful state of their affairs and to urge the Peloponnesians to press the war there even harder than they were doing. The other eleven sailed to Italy, because they had heard that ships loaded with supplies were on their way to the Athenians. They met most of these ships and destroyed them, and in the territory of Caulonia they burned a quantity of shipbuilding timber that had been got ready for the Athenians. The squadron then went to Locri. While they lay at anchor there, one of the merchant ships from Peloponnese came in, carrying Thespian heavy infantry; they took these men on board and sailed along the coast toward home. The Athenians were watching for them at Megara with twenty ships, but could take only one vessel with its crew; the rest got clear away to Syracuse. There was also some skirmishing in the harbor over the piles that the Syracusans had driven into the sea in front of the old docks, so that their ships could lie at anchor inside without being hurt by Athenians sailing up and ramming them. The Athenians brought up a ship of ten thousand talents burden, fitted with wooden turrets and screens. From their boats they fastened ropes around the piles, wrenched them up and broke them, or dived down and sawed them in two. Meanwhile the Syracusans shot at them from the docks, and the Athenians answered from their large vessel, until at last the Athenians had removed most of the piles. But the worst part of the stockade was the part that could not be seen. Some of the piles had been driven in so that they did not show above water, and it was dangerous to sail up, since a ship could run onto them as onto a reef, never having seen them. Yet divers went down and sawed off even these for a reward, although the Syracusans drove in others. Indeed there was no end to the contrivances each side used against the other, as might be expected of two hostile armies facing each other at such short distance; skirmishes and every kind of attempt were constant. Meanwhile the Syracusans sent embassies to the cities, made up of Corinthians, Ambraciots and Lacedaemonians. These were to report the capture of Plemmyrium, and to say that their defeat in the sea-fight was due less to the enemy’s strength than to their own disorder. In general they were to let the cities know that the Syracusans were full of hope, and to ask them to come to their help with ships and troops. For the Athenians were expected with a fresh army, and if the army already there could be destroyed before the other arrived, the war would be at an end.

While the contending parties in Sicily were busy with this, Demosthenes had now gathered the armament with which he was to go to the island. He put out from Aegina and sailed for Peloponnese, where he joined Charicles and the thirty ships of the Athenians. They took on board the heavy infantry from Argos and sailed to Laconia. First they plundered part of Epidaurus Limera; then they landed on the coast of Laconia opposite Cythera, where the temple of Apollo stands, and laid waste part of the country. There they fortified a sort of isthmus, to which the Helots of the Lacedaemonians could desert, and from which plundering raids could be made, as from Pylos. Demosthenes helped to occupy the place, and then sailed straight on to Corcyra to pick up some of the allies there and go on without delay to Sicily. Charicles waited until he had finished fortifying the place; then he left a garrison in it and returned home later with his thirty ships, and with the Argives as well.

In this same summer thirteen hundred targeteers arrived at Athens. They were Thracian swordsmen of the tribe of the Dii, and they were to have sailed to Sicily with Demosthenes. Since they had come too late, the Athenians decided to send them back to Thrace, where they had come from. To keep them for the war against Decelea seemed too expensive, as each man’s pay was a drachma a day. For Decelea had been fortified during this summer by the whole Peloponnesian army, and then occupied, to harass the country, by garrisons from the cities who relieved each other at fixed intervals. It had been doing the Athenians great harm; indeed this occupation, through the destruction of property and the loss of men that came of it, was one of the principal causes of their ruin. Earlier the invasions had been short and had not kept them from enjoying their land for the rest of the time. Now the enemy was fixed in Attica for good. Sometimes it was an attack in force; sometimes it was the regular garrison overrunning the country and making raids for its food; and the Lacedaemonian king, Agis, was in the field and pressing the war hard. The Athenians therefore suffered great harm. They were deprived of their whole country. More than twenty thousand slaves had deserted, a great part of them artisans, and all their sheep and beasts of burden were lost. And since the cavalry rode out daily to Decelea and to guard the country, their horses were either lamed by constant work on rocky ground or wounded by the enemy.

Besides this, provisions from Euboea had before been carried much more quickly overland by Decelea from Oropus; now they were brought at great cost by sea around Sunium. Everything the city required had to be imported from abroad, and instead of a city it became a fortress. Summer and winter the Athenians were worn out by guard duty on the fortifications: by day they served in turns, and by night all together, except the cavalry, at the various military posts or on the wall. But what pressed on them most was that they had two wars at once, and had reached a pitch of frenzy that no one would have believed possible if he had heard of it before it happened. For could anyone have imagined that, even when besieged by the Peloponnesians entrenched in Attica, they would not withdraw from Sicily, but would stay on there and besiege Syracuse in the same way, a town (taken as a town) in no way inferior to Athens? Or that they would so thoroughly overturn the Hellenic estimate of their strength and audacity? At the beginning of the war some thought they might hold out one year, some two, none more than three, if the Peloponnesians invaded their country. Yet here was a people who, seventeen years after the first invasion, and after already suffering all the evils of war, went to Sicily and took on a new war no smaller than the one they already had with the Peloponnesians. These causes, the great losses from Decelea and the other heavy charges that fell upon them, produced their financial embarrassment. It was at this time that they imposed on their subjects, instead of the tribute, a tax of a twentieth on all imports and exports by sea, thinking it would bring in more money. Their expenditure was no longer what it had been at first, but had grown with the war, while their revenues decayed.

So, not wishing to incur expense in their present want of money, they at once sent back the Thracians who had come too late for Demosthenes. They went under the command of Diitrephes, who was instructed to use them, if possible, to injure the enemy on the voyage along the coast, since they were to pass through the Euripus. Diitrephes first landed them at Tanagra, where they hastily snatched some booty. Then in the evening he sailed across the Euripus from Chalcis in Euboea, disembarked in Boeotia and led them against Mycalessus. He spent the night unobserved near the temple of Hermes, not quite two miles from Mycalessus, and at daybreak he assaulted and took the town, which is not a large one. The inhabitants were off their guard and did not expect that anyone would ever come so far from the sea to attack them. The wall was weak, and had fallen down in some places, while in others it had never been built to any height; and the gates had been left open, through their feeling of security. The Thracians burst into Mycalessus, sacked the houses and temples, and butchered the inhabitants. They spared neither youth nor age, but killed everyone they came upon, one after the other, children and women, and even beasts of burden and whatever other living creatures they saw. For the Thracian race, like the bloodiest of the barbarians, is even more so when it has nothing to fear. Everywhere there was confusion and death in all its shapes. In particular they attacked a boys’ school, the largest in the place, which the children had just entered, and massacred them all. In short, the disaster that fell upon the whole town was unsurpassed in magnitude, and unequaled in suddenness and in horror.

Meanwhile the Thebans heard of it and marched to the rescue. They overtook the Thracians before they had gone far, recovered the plunder, and drove them in panic to the Euripus and the sea, where the vessels that had brought them were lying. The greatest slaughter took place while they were embarking, since they did not know how to swim, and the men in the vessels, seeing what was happening on shore, moored them out of bowshot. In the rest of the retreat the Thracians defended themselves quite creditably against the Theban horse, which attacked them first. They dashed out and closed their ranks according to the tactics of their country, and lost only a few men in that part of the affair. A good number who were after plunder were actually caught in the town and put to death. Altogether the Thracians lost two hundred and fifty out of thirteen hundred; the Thebans and the rest who came to the rescue lost about twenty, troopers and heavy infantry, among them Scirphondas, one of the Boeotarchs. The Mycalessians lost a large proportion of their population.

Mycalessus thus suffered a calamity as lamentable, for its extent, as any that happened in the war. Demosthenes, whom we left sailing to Corcyra after building the fort in Laconia, now found a merchantman lying at Phea in Elis, in which the Corinthian heavy infantry were to cross to Sicily. He destroyed the ship, but the men escaped and later got another, in which they continued their voyage. After this he arrived at Zacynthus and Cephallenia and took a body of heavy infantry on board. He also sent for some of the Messenians from Naupactus, and crossed to the opposite coast of Acarnania, to Alyzia and to Anactorium, which was held by the Athenians. While he was in these parts, Eurymedon met him, returning from Sicily, where he had been sent, as has been mentioned, during the winter, with the money for the army. Eurymedon told him the news, and said also that he had heard at sea that the Syracusans had taken Plemmyrium. Here, too, Conon came to them, the commander at Naupactus. He brought word that the twenty-five Corinthian ships stationed opposite him, far from giving up the war, were planning an engagement, and he begged them to send him some ships, since his own eighteen were no match for the enemy’s twenty-five. Demosthenes and Eurymedon therefore sent ten of their best sailers with Conon to reinforce the squadron at Naupactus, and meanwhile prepared to muster their forces. Eurymedon, who was now the colleague of Demosthenes and had turned back because of his appointment, sailed to Corcyra to tell them to man fifteen ships and enlist heavy infantry; Demosthenes raised slingers and darters from the parts around Acarnania.

Meanwhile the envoys already mentioned, who had gone from Syracuse to the cities after the capture of Plemmyrium, had succeeded in their mission and were about to bring the army they had collected. Nicias got wind of it, and sent to the Centoripae, the Alicyaeans and others of the friendly Sicels who held the passes, telling them not to let the enemy through but to combine to prevent their passing; there was no other way by which they could even attempt it, since the Agrigentines would not give them passage through their country. In keeping with this request the Sicels laid a triple ambush for the Siceliots on their march. They attacked suddenly, while the Siceliots were off their guard, and killed about eight hundred of them and all the envoys except the Corinthian one, who conducted the fifteen hundred survivors to Syracuse.

About the same time the Camarinaeans also came to help Syracuse, with five hundred heavy infantry, three hundred darters and as many archers, while the Geloans sent crews for five ships, four hundred darters and two hundred horse. Indeed almost the whole of Sicily, except the Agrigentines, who were neutral, now stopped merely watching events, as it had done until then, and actively joined Syracuse against the Athenians.

After the Sicel disaster the Syracusans put off any immediate attack on the Athenians. Demosthenes and Eurymedon, whose forces from Corcyra and the mainland were now ready, crossed the Ionian Gulf with their whole armament to the Iapygian promontory. From there they started and touched at the Choerades Isles, off Iapygia, where they took on board a hundred and fifty Iapygian darters of the Messapian tribe. They renewed an old friendship with Artas the chief, who had supplied them with the darters, and arrived at Metapontium in Italy. Here they persuaded their allies the Metapontines to send three hundred darters and two galleys with them, and with this reinforcement they coasted on to Thurii. There they found that the party hostile to Athens had recently been expelled by a revolution, and so they stayed to muster and review the whole army, to see if any had been left behind, and to prevail on the Thurians to join their expedition wholeheartedly and, in the circumstances in which they found themselves, to conclude a defensive and offensive alliance with the Athenians.

About the same time the Peloponnesians in the twenty-five ships stationed opposite the squadron at Naupactus, to protect the passage of the transports to Sicily, had got ready for an engagement. They manned some additional vessels, so as to be little inferior in number to the Athenians, and anchored off Erineus in Achaia, in the Rhypic country. The place where they lay is shaped like a crescent. The land forces furnished by the Corinthians and their allies on the spot came up and took position on the headlands projecting on either side, while the fleet, under Polyanthes, a Corinthian, held the space between and blocked the entrance. The Athenians under Diphilus now sailed out against them from Naupactus with thirty-three ships. At first the Corinthians did not move; at length they thought they saw their opportunity, raised the signal, advanced and engaged the Athenians. After an obstinate struggle the Corinthians lost three ships. Without sinking any altogether, they disabled seven of the enemy’s: these were struck prow to prow and had their foreships stove in by the Corinthian vessels, whose cheeks had been strengthened for this very purpose. The action was of this even character, and either party could claim the victory (although the Athenians became masters of the wrecks, because the wind drove them out to sea and the Corinthians did not put out again to meet them). The two sides then parted. There was no pursuit and no prisoners were taken on either side; the Corinthians and Peloponnesians who were fighting near the shore escaped easily, and none of the Athenian vessels had been sunk. The Athenians now sailed back to Naupactus, and the Corinthians immediately set up a trophy as victors, because they had disabled more of the enemy’s ships. Moreover they held that they had not been worsted, for the very same reason that their opponent held that he had not been victorious. The Corinthians considered that they were conquerors if they were not decidedly conquered, and the Athenians thought themselves vanquished because they were not decidedly victorious. However, when the Peloponnesians sailed off and their land forces had dispersed, the Athenians also set up a trophy as victors in Achaia, about two miles and a quarter from Erineus, the Corinthian station.

This was how the action at Naupactus ended. To return to Demosthenes and Eurymedon. The Thurians were now ready to join the expedition with seven hundred heavy infantry and three hundred darters. The two generals ordered the ships to sail along the coast to the territory of Croton, and meanwhile held a review of all the land forces on the river Sybaris, and then led them through the Thurian country. When they arrived at the river Hylias, the Crotonians sent them a message saying that they would not allow the army to pass through their country. So the Athenians went down toward the shore and bivouacked near the sea and the mouth of the Hylias, where the fleet also met them. The next day they embarked and sailed along the coast, touching at all the cities except Locri, until they came to Petra in the territory of Rhegium.

Meanwhile the Syracusans heard of their approach and resolved to make a second attempt with their fleet and with the other forces on shore, which they had been collecting for this very purpose, in order to do something before the Athenians arrived. The former sea-fight had suggested several improvements, which they now adopted in equipping their navy. Among them, they cut down their prows to a smaller compass to make them more solid, and made their cheeks stouter. From these they ran stays into the vessels’ sides, for a length of six cubits inside and outside, just as the Corinthians had altered their prows before engaging the squadron at Naupactus. The Syracusans thought this would give them an advantage over the Athenian vessels, which were not built with equal strength but were slight in the bows. For the Athenians were more used to sailing around and charging the enemy’s side than to meeting him prow to prow. The Syracusans also counted it in their favor that the battle would be in the great harbor, with many ships in not much room. By charging prow to prow they would stave in the enemy’s bows, striking with solid and stout beaks against hollow and weak ones. Secondly, the Athenians for want of room would be unable to use their favorite maneuver of breaking the line or sailing around: the Syracusans would do their best not to let them do the one, and want of room would prevent them doing the other. This charging prow to prow, which had until now been thought a want of skill in a helmsman, would be the Syracusans’ chief maneuver, as the one they would find most useful. For the Athenians, if repulsed, would not be able to back water in any direction except toward the shore, and only for a little way, in the little space in front of their own camp. The rest of the harbor would be commanded by the Syracusans. And the Athenians, if hard pressed, would crowd together in a small space, all toward the same point, and run foul of one another and fall into disorder. This was, in fact, the thing that did the Athenians most harm in all the sea-fights, since they did not have, as the Syracusans did, the whole harbor to retreat over. As for sailing around into the open sea, that would be impossible, with the Syracusans holding the way out and in, especially as Plemmyrium would be hostile to them and the mouth of the harbor was not large.

With these contrivances suited to their skill and ability, and now more confident after the previous sea-fight, the Syracusans attacked by land and sea at once. Gylippus led out the town force a little earlier and brought it up to the wall of the Athenians where it faced the city. The force from the Olympieum, that is to say the heavy infantry there together with the horse and the light troops of the Syracusans, advanced against the wall from the opposite side. The ships of the Syracusans and their allies sailed out immediately afterward. The Athenians at first thought they were to be attacked by land only, and it was not without alarm that they saw the fleet suddenly approaching as well. Some formed up on the walls and in front of them against the advancing enemy; some marched out in haste against the numbers of horse and darters coming from the Olympieum and from outside; others manned the ships or rushed down to the beach to oppose the enemy. When the ships were manned they put out with seventy-five ships against about eighty of the Syracusans.

They spent a great part of the day advancing, retreating and skirmishing with each other, and neither side gained any advantage worth speaking of, except that the Syracusans sank one or two of the Athenian vessels. Then they parted, and the land force at the same time withdrew from the lines. The next day the Syracusans remained quiet and gave no sign of what they would do. But Nicias saw that the battle had been a drawn one and expected them to attack again. He compelled the captains to refit any ships that had suffered, and he moored merchant vessels in front of the stockade that the Athenians had driven into the sea before their ships. These served in place of an enclosed harbor, and were placed about two hundred feet from each other, so that any ship that was hard pressed could retreat in safety and sail out again at leisure. These preparations occupied the Athenians all day until nightfall.

The next day the Syracusans began operations at an earlier hour, but with the same plan of attack by land and sea. The rivals spent a great part of the day as before, facing each other and skirmishing. At last Ariston, son of Pyrrhicus, a Corinthian and the ablest helmsman in the Syracusan service, persuaded their naval commanders to send to the officials in the city. They were to tell them to move the market down to the sea as quickly as they could, and to oblige everyone to bring whatever food he had and sell it there. This would let the commanders land the crews and have dinner at once close to the ships, and shortly afterward, the very same day, attack the Athenians again when they were not expecting it.

In compliance with this advice a messenger was sent and the market was got ready. Then the Syracusans suddenly backed water and withdrew to the town, where they landed at once and took their dinner on the spot. The Athenians supposed that they had returned to the town because they felt beaten. They disembarked at their leisure and set about getting their dinners and attending to other business, thinking they were done with fighting for that day. Suddenly the Syracusans had manned their ships and were sailing against them again. The Athenians, in great confusion and most of them fasting, got on board and with great difficulty put out to meet them. For some time both sides stayed on the defensive without engaging. Then the Athenians resolved not to let themselves be worn out by waiting where they were, but to attack without delay, and with a cheer they went into action. The Syracusans received them, and charging prow to prow as they had planned, stove in a great part of the Athenian foreships with the strength of their beaks. The darters on the decks also did great damage to the Athenians. But still greater damage was done by the Syracusans who went about in small boats, ran in under the oars of the Athenian galleys, sailed against their sides, and from there discharged their darts at the sailors.

At last, fighting hard in this way, the Syracusans won the victory, and the Athenians turned and fled between the merchantmen to their own station. The Syracusan ships pursued them as far as the merchantmen, where they were stopped by the beams armed with dolphins that hung from those vessels over the passage. Two of the Syracusan vessels went too near in the excitement of victory and were destroyed, one of them being taken with its crew. The Syracusans sank seven of the Athenian vessels, disabled many, took most of the men prisoner and killed others. Then they retired and set up trophies for both engagements. They were now confident of having a decided superiority by sea, and by no means despaired of equal success by land.
